definition: Obliterate means to destroy completely, leaving no trace.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obliterate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obliterate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three laser sessions obliterated the tattoo, and the skin healed so evenly the artist could not say where it had been.
A smudge only blurs the mark — anyone can still see something was there — while obliterate leaves nothing to show anything ever existed.
Erase goes further than smudge — the mark itself comes off the page — but obliterate claims the most: nothing left to show anything was ever there.

To blot out is to cover or soak a mark until it cannot be seen — the ink-and-paper picture obliterate grew from. But a blotted mark is hidden, not gone; lift the cover and traces remain. Obliterate insists that nothing at all survives to find.

Expunge is the official's word: a name or a charge struck from the record, deliberately and by someone with authority. Obliterate is physical and total — shells, lasers, centuries of weather — erasing the thing itself, not just its entry in a file.

The one-room school pushed literacy above all else: every farm child reading by eight and writing by nine.
Obliterate means to destroy completely, leaving no trace.

The shelling of 1916 obliterated nine villages around Verdun so completely that when the war ended there was nothing to rebuild — no walls, no wells, not a street line traceable under the leaf litter.
France never rebuilt them.
Each site keeps a signboard in the forest, naming a town that exists now only as a name.
Obliterate is the exact word for what the shelling did, because it means to destroy completely, leaving no trace — and the no trace clause is the whole word.
The Latin beneath it meant to blot out the letters: erasure so total the page forgets the ink.
Damage leaves wreckage to point at; even demolish leaves rubble.
Obliterate leaves absence.
Obliterate is the totality word: reach for it only when nothing is left to point at.

Its unit-mates divide destruction's labor — raze levels a building but leaves the rubble and the lot; eradicate wipes out something living or spreading, to the last case; obliterate erases even the last signs.
If a trace survives, the word has been overspent.

When the volcano's mudflow finally stopped, the valley where the village of San Marcos had stood for three centuries was a smooth gray plain.
Archaeologists arrived a decade later expecting buried walls, the way ash had once sealed ancient towns for later discovery.
Instead they found that the boiling lahar had obliterated the site: it had not covered the village but scoured it, dragging stone, timber, and even the street grid down the valley.
Ground-penetrating radar returned nothing; test trenches turned up river gravel where the plaza should have been.
The team's final report was one page long, and its conclusion was blunt: there is nothing here to excavate, because nothing remains.
